headline: Israeli president selects Gadi Eisenkot to attempt government formation
standfirst: Israel's president has tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government, bypassing incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after an inconclusive election.
keyPoints: President Isaac Herzog asked Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government on Saturday.
Eisenkot received endorsements from 67 lawmakers, compared to 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu.
Neither main bloc secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority in the October 27 election.
Eisenkot has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension.

paragraphs: Israel's political landscape shifted dramatically on Saturday when President Isaac Herzog selected opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the nation's next government. The decision bypasses current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu following an inconclusive general election held on October 27, which left both major political blocs short of a parliamentary majority. President Herzog informed Eisenkot of the appointment during a meeting, with a formal mandate ceremony scheduled to take place at the presidential residence on Sunday.

The presidential spokesperson confirmed that Eisenkot secured endorsements from 67 lawmakers across various political factions, while Prime Minister Netanyahu received support from 46 members of the Knesset. This higher count gave the president a clear indication of where parliamentary recommendations lay following a week of intensive consultations with party leaders. Eisenkot, a former military chief and leader of the Yashar party, now faces a demanding 28-day window to negotiate a workable coalition that can survive a confidence vote.

The electoral outcome left the legislature deeply divided after voters went to the polls in late October. Netanyahu's right-wing and religious alliance captured 53 seats, remaining the largest ideological bloc, but falling short of the 61-seat threshold required in the 120-member Knesset. Meanwhile, Eisenkot's four-party centre-left and right-wing alliance secured 48 seats, and Arab-led parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel achieved a record 19 seats in the parliament.

sections.heading: Political background and electoral deadlock
paragraphs: The path to this political crisis stems from the October 27 general election, which failed to deliver a decisive mandate to any single political camp. Israel's proportional representation system frequently results in fragmented parliaments where smaller factions hold significant leverage over coalition talks. Prime Minister Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving leader, has governed through various religious-nationalist coalitions but found his support eroded during the recent vote.

Gadi Eisenkot entered national politics in 2022 after a lengthy military career that included serving as Israel's military chief from 2015 to 2019. Following the outbreak of the Gaza conflict in October 2023, he briefly participated in Netanyahu's wartime cabinet as an observer before returning to the opposition benches. His public profile and security credentials have been heavily shaped by his military background, alongside personal family tragedies during the ongoing conflict.

To achieve the necessary 61 seats in the Knesset, Eisenkot must navigate complex parliamentary arithmetic and deep ideological divides. His potential pathways include forming a minority administration with external support from Arab-led parties, reaching an agreement with ultra-Orthodox factions, or establishing a unity government with Netanyahu. Analysts view these options as difficult to achieve given longstanding political animosities and declared campaign red lines.

sections.heading: Differing stances and intense rhetoric
paragraphs: The decision by President Herzog drew starkly different reactions from the rival political camps across the country. Arab-led parties, which won an unprecedented 19 seats, chose to endorse Eisenkot primarily to prevent the continuation of Netanyahu's administration. Senior figures within the Arab-led factions expressed strong opposition to Netanyahu and his far-right allies, such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

Prime Minister Netanyahu strongly condemned the prospect of an opposition-led administration backed by Arab politicians, issuing warnings via video message before the presidential announcement. He argued that such an arrangement would threaten national security and dismantle the state from within. In response, critics dismissed these warnings, trading sharp accusations over political extremism and leadership credentials.

Despite receiving endorsements from Arab-led lawmakers, Eisenkot has publicly ruled out formally including them in a coalition government. Analysts note that bridging these gaps will require careful negotiation to satisfy campaign promises while building enough parliamentary backing to pass a crucial confidence vote in the Knesset.

sections.heading: Potential wider implications for the region
paragraphs: The outcome of these coalition negotiations carries profound implications for Israel's domestic policies and its standing in the international community. Netanyahu's previous governance involved close alignment with far-right figures who have faced Western sanctions for actions in the West Bank. Eisenkot has previously voiced criticism of surging settler violence against Palestinians, which has strained relations between Israel and various Western allies.

Domestically, a transition of power could alter the trajectory of governance after years of continuous leadership under Netanyahu. The inclusion or exclusion of ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties will redefine social priorities, military policies, and legislative agendas inside the Knesset. Observers suggest that any government formed under Eisenkot will likely focus heavily on security management while attempting to mend fractured diplomatic ties.

The broader regional environment remains highly volatile as the political maneuvering unfolds in Jerusalem. The decisions made during the upcoming coalition talks will directly influence Israel's military strategies, governance in the occupied territories, and interactions with international partners watching the political transition closely.

sections.heading: Next steps and strict deadlines
paragraphs: Following his official receipt of the mandate, Eisenkot holds an initial period of 28 days to construct a viable governing coalition. President Herzog holds the authority to grant a single 14-day extension if negotiations require additional time to reach a final agreement among prospective coalition partners. Securing the backing of at least 61 lawmakers remains the absolute requirement for establishing a stable administration.

Should Eisenkot fail to meet the deadline and secure a majority confidence vote, the political process moves to alternative candidates. President Herzog would nominate a second individual to try forming a government, and if that attempt also fails, a parliamentary majority can back a third candidate for a final 14-day period. The entire sequence has a strict limit of approximately 100 days.

If all attempts to establish a government ultimately fail, Israel will face a mandatory new election called within 90 days. In that scenario, Benjamin Netanyahu would remain in office serving as the caretaker prime minister while the country prepares to return to the ballot box.

highlight: President Herzog held consultations with political parties this week to decide who he would appoint to form a government after neither side secured a majority in the October 27 general election.
socialSummary: Israel's president tasks former military chief Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government, bypassing Benjamin Netanyahu.
